title: Do not covet
hook: the only commandment about desire alone

segments.voice: Yesterday, the truthful witness: no gossip, no spin, no harmful half-truths about someone who isn't there. Your line was speak truly. Did you find the kind true thing to say? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

House. Wife. Manservant. Maidservant. Ox. Donkey. The commandment piles them up one after another, the way an eye moves down a street, over a fence, into somebody else's yard. And then, as if it knows the list could never be finished, it ends with: anything that is your neighbor's. Read the earlier commandments and they mostly name things a person does: steal, kill, speak falsely. This one names something that can happen without anyone moving a muscle. Some readers point out that it's about desire alone. Today: do not covet.

Here it is in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's." Notice what it doesn't forbid. Wanting a house isn't the problem. Wanting your neighbor's house is: the desire that looks at someone else's life and decides it should have been yours. The apostle Paul picks out this commandment when he describes what the law showed him about himself. In his letter to the Romans he writes: "I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet." Some readers put it this way: his hands might stay clean, but his wanting was another matter, and this commandment brought it into the light. So the Christian answer isn't to stop wanting. It's contentment, and Paul is honest that it takes practice. To the Philippians he writes: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned. Not born with it. The letter to the Hebrews gives the ground under it: be content with such things as ye have, for God has said, "I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee." That's the turn. Coveting says my life is short of something, and the neighbor has it. Contentment says what I have is enough, because I'm not left alone with it. It doesn't mean pretending you lack nothing. It means you can see your neighbor's good things and leave them where they are.

Here's the practice: be glad for someone's good fortune. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who has something you've wanted: a house, a job, a marriage, an easy kind of confidence. Let the picture come clearly, and notice whatever stirs in you, without scolding it. Then, on each slow breath, wish them well in it. Their house, kept warm. Their work, going well. If you pray, you can thank God for what they've been given. The bell holds the time.
Do not covet. Don't set your desire on what belongs to your neighbor. The commandment that reaches past the hands to the wanting itself.
Your line: enough is enough. Today, when you catch yourself looking over someone's fence, name one thing on your own side of it that is already enough. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Christians learn this commandment with the rest of the Ten Commandments in catechism and Sunday school, and examine themselves by it in prayer; Paul's words on contentment in Philippians 4 are sometimes read alongside it.

fork.setup: you're Paul, writing to the Romans about what the law showed you about your own heart. which commandment do you name?
options: thou shalt not bear false witness.
fork.reveal: Romans 7:7: "I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet." the commandment about wanting showed him his wanting.

original.note: Hebrew, from Exodus 20:17: do not covet, do not set your desire on it.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be jealous of the neighbors.
what it means: don't let your desire settle on what is theirs; learn contentment with what is yours.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 20:17 lists the house before the wife; Deuteronomy 5:21 puts the wife first, and the King James there says desire for her and covet for the house.

notes: The index hook says 'the only commandment about desire alone'. Per the claims rule this is not stated by the cited text, so the script softens it to 'some readers point out that it's about desire alone' and 'the earlier commandments mostly name things a person does'. Consider revising the index hook.
Hook lists 'Donkey' for KJV 'ass' in the spoken list; the full KJV wording appears in the teach quotation.
Hebrews 13:5 is partly paraphrased ('be content with such things as ye have') and partly quoted; confirm.

Trapdoor: Deuteronomy 5:21 KJV reads 'Neither shalt thou desire thy neighbour's wife, neither shalt thou covet thy neighbour's house'; confirm the ordering claim against Exodus 20:17. This difference is part of why some churches divide the coveting commandment; the script doesn't say so (numbering covered on day 1183).
Original: לֹא תַחְמֹד (Exodus 20:17); confirm vocalization and pronunciation.

Editor pass: teach's flat claims that this commandment 'caught' Paul and that he 'could keep his hands clean' (not in Romans 7) recast as Paul naming it plus 'some readers put it this way'; fork setup reworded to match; howItsDone 'often read' softened to 'sometimes read'.
